1:
Keil and Delitzsch open with the shape of the whole chapter: the Jews fought on the day both edicts had named, supported by the royal officials; Susa alone was granted a second day at the queen's request; and because the two fights ended a day apart, one part of the nation rests on the fourteenth and the other on the fifteenth. Henry frames the same day as a fair trial of skill, since neither side was surprised, both had long notice, and neither could call the other rebels, both being supported by the royal authority.

Why anyone still attacked is asked by three of them. Henry reports the Chaldee paraphrase, that none appeared against the Jews but Amalekites only, infatuated and hardened as Pharaoh was, and adds that Haman's fall had exasperated rather than convinced his party, his sons having vowed to carry on their father's designs. Gill says the same of the five hundred, that they were men of Haman's faction headed by his ten sons and taking the decree as their occasion of revenge, the Targum calling them princes of the house of Amalek. Clarke finds it strange that in a city where the king's mind must have been well known, five hundred could be found to rise against those he befriended.

Whether the Jews kept within the letter of their commission is the one real dispute. Ellicott doubts it. They had the whole executive of the empire on their side, the second edict was treated as repealing the first, and a people so lately in fear and now in favour at court were probably resolved to use their opportunity while they had it; who could object, he asks, so long as they did nothing against the authorities, and the numbers later reported show what use they made of it. Clarke reads the record the other way, that it does not appear the Jews slew any person who did not rise up to destroy them, and Wesley agrees, taking those killed for men who would have watched every opportunity against them. Henry rests the defence on necessity, that they stood for their lives under the law of self-preservation as well as the king's decree.

On why they prevailed the accounts converge. Henry credits their acting in concert rather than family by family, and turns the tag that forces act most powerfully when combined against the Jews of his own day, numerous and rich in many places and yet despicable because too selfish to incorporate. Gill notes that the rulers did more than permit them, the word meaning that they extolled and lifted them up, and that Mordecai was by now the chief minister of state; Ellicott observes that the verb rendered helped is literally lifted up. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the idiom, that no one stood before them because the fear of them had fallen upon all people.

The ten sons draw a different kind of attention. Keil and Delitzsch describe the column in which their names are printed, meant only to make them prominent and easy to count, and report what the later rabbis made of it, a sign that they should never rise again, or that they hung one above another on a single line; the small letters in three of the names they leave unexplained, since what those indicate is not known. Henry has the custom from the other side, that the reader of this book at the feast takes all ten names in one breath because they are held to have died in one moment. On the untouched spoil he offers three reasons: a contempt of worldly wealth in imitation of Abraham refusing the spoils of Sodom; proof that they sought their preservation and not their enrichment; and humanity, since they might have destroyed the women and little ones and instead left them what would keep them alive.
10:
The refusal of the spoil is read by all three who mention it as deliberate self-clearing. Clarke says they stood for their lives and gave full proof that they sought their own safety and not their enemies' property, though the decree in their favour had expressly given them authority to take it. Ellicott confirms the permission in a line, that they might have done it according to the edict. Wesley adds the motive and the beneficiary together: they left it to their enemies' children, so that what they did should appear to be done not out of malice or covetousness but out of necessity, and by that great law of self-preservation.

How the tally reached the king Gill will not settle. Either the king ordered it, wanting to know how many enemies the Jews had in the city and how many of his own subjects had fallen, or it was brought officiously by others with the intention of irritating him against the Jews. Wesley hears the question about the provinces as a concession rather than a complaint: in those, doubtless, many more were slain, so the petition has been fully granted, and yet if anything further is wanted the king stands ready.

The second day is where the commentators part company, and the division is moral rather than textual. Ellicott refuses to defend it. Before the first day's slaughter was over the Jews were plainly out of danger, the sympathies of the court were entirely with them and the king's officers had taken their part, so that after five hundred killed in the capital alone they were masters of the situation; he therefore does not hesitate to call the fresh action needless butchery, and says that because Esther was a person God made use of for a great purpose we are not called upon to tone down the black spots in her history. He allows only that she is not to be judged by the Christian standard, since the older teaching said that vengeance belonged to God but it took the newer to bring that truth home. Wesley answers the objection Ellicott dismisses, supposing that the worst of the enemies had hidden themselves for the one day, after which the commission would expire and they would confidently return home. Clarke argues the same from information rather than from probability, that Esther had likely learned from Mordecai how many had escaped the first day; three hundred more were found, eight hundred in all, and the city was purged.

On the ten sons the question is what hanging adds to men already dead. Clarke notes that they had been slain the day before and that the request is for them to be exposed as a terror to those who sought the Jews' destruction. Wesley says the same in harsher terms, for their greater infamy and the terror of any who should presume to abuse the king in the like manner. Keil and Delitzsch supply the practice behind it, the dead bodies nailed up for the sake of the greater disgrace after the Hebrew and Persian custom that the law of the hanged malefactor also assumes. Ellicott alone calls it what he thinks it is, a gratuitous outrage on the dead.

Keil and Delitzsch close with a point of construction the others pass over. The decree given at Susa is not the order for the hanging but the permission to fight on the morrow, since it is that permission which accounts for the Jews assembling again on the fourteenth, while the hanging is related in a subordinate clause by a simple perfect. They also notice the odd placement of the rest from their enemies in the verse about the provinces, coming before rather than after the slaughter, and explain it as the narrator's wish to point out at once how the matter ended.
16:
The figure for the provinces is the one place in the chapter where the text itself is doubted. Ellicott notes that the Greek version gives fifteen thousand rather than seventy-five, and thinks the smaller number perhaps the likelier. He then sets the whole episode in a wider frame by quoting Bishop Wordsworth, that the history shows the recklessness of human life which then prevailed among the sovereigns of the East, even towards their own subjects, and that it displays what would have followed for civilisation had Ahasuerus won at Salamis; the hand of God, on that reading, wrought for the deliverance of mankind in the Greek straits as well as for the preservation of the Jews in the provinces of Persia.

Keil and Delitzsch keep to the arithmetic of the two dates. The Jews of Susa were still fighting on both the thirteenth and the fourteenth and did not rest until the fifteenth, so they made the later day their day of rejoicing, while those elsewhere finished on the thirteenth and kept the fourteenth. The statement about the country towns is introduced by a word meaning therefore, which they take as the narrator's way of presenting the custom as the result of what has just been told rather than as an independent fact; and they remark that the written form of the word for the unwalled places looks like an Aramaic variant. Clarke states the Susa side of it flatly, that the two days were spent in slaying their enemies and the third in rest.

Gill supplies the rule the later synagogue drew from the difference, reporting it from Jarchi. Every place walled from the days of Joshua, whether inside the land or out of it, reads this book on the fifteenth of Adar and is called a walled town, even if its walls are now gone; a place unwalled in those days reads on the fourteenth and is called a city, even if it is walled now. Shushan is the exception that proves how the rule was framed, since it was not walled in Joshua's day and yet reads on the fifteenth, because in it a miracle was done. Ellicott approaches the same distinction through the words rather than the custom, the two terms used of the country towns being virtually one word, meaning places undefended by bulwarks, and the same term standing elsewhere in contrast with fenced cities.

On what the day was for, Clarke is the fullest. The villagers joined their rest to the preceding day and made it a time of festivity and of sending portions to each other, by which he understands that the rich sent portions of what was killed for the occasion to the poor, so that they too might be able to keep the day; as the sorrow had been general, so also might the joy be. Ellicott adds the outcome, that both the fourteenth and the fifteenth are now kept as the feast, the earlier day being the chief.

Clarke also records a textual observation that unsettles the section he has just expounded. The ancient Itala version omits the whole of these nineteen verses, and he does not smooth the difficulty over but puts the question it raises directly, whether they were originally in the book at all. He leaves it as a query and does not answer it, and none of the others takes it up.
20:
What Mordecai wrote, and how much of it, is the first question. Gill takes it for the transactions of those two days with their causes, together with the letter that follows, and notes that some conclude from this that he was the penman of the book; he allows that he might have been, but will not have it follow necessarily. Clarke supposes the part written by Mordecai ends about here and that what comes after was added by Ezra or the men of the Great Synagogue, though he grants the words may refer only to the letters sent into the provinces; either way the rest of the chapter is recapitulation with the institution of the feast attached.

Henry turns the authorship question into a comparison that he does not resolve in Mordecai's favour. Nehemiah at every turn notices divine Providence and the good hand of his God upon him; Mordecai never so much as mentions the name of God in the whole story. The difference he lays to the two places: Nehemiah wrote at Jerusalem, where religion was in fashion and an air of it appeared in common conversation, and Mordecai at Shushan, where policy reigned more than piety, and he wrote according to the genius of the place. Henry commends the one style and means to imitate it, and takes the other's lesson too, that men may be truly devout without abounding in the shows of devotion, so we must not judge or despise our brethren. He adds that the very absence of the language of Canaan has led many to think the book not Mordecai's at all but an extract from the Persian journals.

On the choice of days Henry makes the observation the others leave alone: they did not keep the day when they fought but the days when they rested, as the sabbath was appointed not on the day God finished his work but on the day he rested from it. He notes that the feast falls a month before the passover, so that the first and last month of the year both keep the memory of a deliverance, and that two whole days were spent in thanksgiving without being thought too many. He disputes the later custom of fasting on the thirteenth, since the fasting belonged to the day of distress and was not to be continued once the fast had been turned into gladness.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the settling of it as a ratification rather than a command. The people had already begun by keeping both days; Mordecai wrote that this should be made an annual custom, and they agreed to do it in consequence of his letters. Ellicott marks the one thing actually added, that the provinces had already made the fourteenth their day of gladness and that what Mordecai now enjoins is the keeping of the fifteenth as well. Gill glosses the ground of the whole, that these were the days on which they rested from enemies who had risen up against them.

Henry reads the three prescriptions as ascending. It was to be a day of cheerfulness, since when God gives cause to rejoice there is no reason to hide the joy; a day of generosity, the portions sent between friends knitting them closer by the common deliverance; and a day of charity, the gifts going to the poor and not to rich neighbours, so that thanksgiving and almsgiving go together. He then records what the feast became, on the testimony of Jewish writers themselves, commonly celebrated with gluttony and drunkenness and excess of riot, the Talmud saying outright that a man should drink at Purim until he cannot tell the difference between cursing Haman and blessing Mordecai. A religious feast turned into a revel draws from him the tag that what is best becomes, when corrupted, the worst.
23:
Gill is careful about what kind of obligation the Jews took on. They engaged to keep the two days annually not in a religious but in a civil way, not as parts of worship nor as additions to the law, but in commemoration of a civil benefit received. He then reports that the scruple was raised anyway in later times, eighty five elders, more than thirty of them prophets, having been distressed about the matter for fear it was an innovation. Clarke measures the undertaking by its result instead: Mordecai wrote to bind them, their successors and their proselytes to an annual feast, they undertook it, and it has been observed among them in all the places of their dispersion from that day to this without any interruption.

The recapitulation of Haman's device raises a small textual question that two of them answer the same way. Keil and Delitzsch argue that the clause about coming before the king is impersonal, and means when the matter came, not when Esther came, since she is not named anywhere in the context; the order that followed was given in writing, that the wicked device should return upon its author's own head. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the printed page, pointing out that the name stands in italics in the English version because it is not in the Hebrew, which says only and on her or its coming; to make the pronoun mean Esther seems harsh when she has not been mentioned for some time, so he prefers the impersonal reading.

Why the feast bears the name it does is settled without dispute. Gill and Clarke both take Purim from the lot Haman cast to find the month and the day most favourable to his design, and Wesley notes that the word is Persian. Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the two clauses that follow, the first giving the reason for the name and the second opening a fresh sentence that runs to the end of the section and explains how the observance became general; two grounds are stated there, the written injunction of Mordecai and the fact that the people had seen and experienced the thing themselves. They add that the phrase about the days not failing is a periphrasis for inviolably.

On who is bound, the commentators move from the text to the practice. Wesley explains why the proselytes are included, since they were obliged to submit to other Jewish laws and had enjoyed the benefit of this deliverance, without which the nation and its religion would have been in great measure extinct. Gill quotes the canon that makes the obligation exhaustive: priests, Levites, Nethinims, Israelites, men, women, proselytes and servants made free are all obliged to read the book, and little ones are trained up to read it. Ellicott describes the observance as it stands, kept on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar with the preceding day as a fast, the whole book read through in the synagogue service, a custom he traces back at least to the Christian era on the evidence of Josephus and the older Jewish records.

Gill closes the section with a point of geography taken from Aben Ezra. The words about every province and every city are not decoration but precaution, set down lest a man should think himself unbound where there are no Jews; wherever he may be, he is obliged to keep it. Keil and Delitzsch put the same permanence in terms of the grammar, the participles about remembering and keeping still depending on the clause that makes the observance perpetual, so that the days are not to pass away among the Jews nor their remembrance to cease among their seed.
29:
The force of this second letter is agreed. Gill observes that Mordecai had before only recommended the festival and that the queen now gave it her sanction and laid her obligation on the Jews, guessing that some had been backward or had neglected it; he reports a Jewish chronologer dating the letter to the following year, and the older Targum's account that what they wrote was the whole volume, set down so as to put the deliverance in the strongest light. Wesley says the same more plainly, that the former letter recommended and this one enjoins, because it was now not Mordecai's act only but the act of all the Jews binding themselves and their posterity. Keil and Delitzsch translate the phrase as writing with all strength, which is to say very forcibly, and read the purpose as giving the letter's contents the force of law. Clarke adds only that the two of them had the king's licence and that their own authority was great.

Which letter is being counted as the first is not agreed. Keil and Delitzsch take this to be the second with reference to the one Mordecai had already sent through the provinces. Ellicott counts differently: the first, he thinks, must be the one Esther obtained from the king, so that the second is Mordecai's own, here confirmed in a more authoritative way. Neither treats the point as trivial, since it decides whether the letter now described is a fresh instrument or the ratification of an earlier one.

The clause about fasting is the crux of the section. Ellicott admits the words about the fastings and the cry come in awkwardly, and that because the Greek version passes them over some have doubted whether they belong here; but all the Hebrew copies and the other ancient versions keep them, so he concludes that the Jews throughout the empire had instituted fasts and lamentations beyond what Mordecai enjoined, and connects this with the fast now kept on the thirteenth of Adar. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same sense from the suffix, which relates to the days of Purim and can therefore only mean portions of time within them, so that the fasting was appointed inside the festival rather than beside it. Wesley supplies the occasion the words look back to, the calamities decreed against the whole nation, for the removing of which not only Esther and the Jews in Shushan but all the rest in every place had fled to God with fasting and strong cries. Ellicott notes besides that one Hebrew verb stands behind the three English words for confirming, enjoining and decreeing, and that its force is simply to fix or settle.

Clarke draws attention to who is absent from the transaction. There is no mention of the approbation of any high priest, nor of any authority beyond that of Mordecai and Esther; the king could not join in such a business, having nothing to do with a religion that was not the religion of his country.

What the book is that received the decree divides them at the last. Clarke reports the versions rather than choosing between them, the Vulgate giving the clause a strange turn by making it cover everything contained in the history called Esther, the Targum saying that the roll was transcribed in this book, the Syriac agreeing with the Hebrew and the Greek not differing much. Ellicott weighs the same options and is dissatisfied with the obvious one, since the book is hardly a natural way for an author to refer to the work he is writing and no similar case can be adduced; he mentions the suggestion of a book composed at the time about the festival, and Canon Rawlinson's identification of it with the chronicles of the kings, which at least agrees with the use of the word everywhere else in this history.
